blocks.text:
Design the counting system behind the like button, the small feature sitting underneath a photo, post, or video that has to survive one very specific, very brutal kind of load: a single post going viral and receiving tens of thousands of likes per second, every single one of them pointed at the exact same counter. This is a narrower, deeper problem than designing the whole of Instagram, it deliberately zooms in on one hard sub-problem, the same way a real system design interview often asks you to go deep on one specific mechanism rather than sketch an entire product. The two things that make this genuinely hard are that a single database row being incremented that fast will become a serialization bottleneck no matter how good the database is, and that the same user tapping like twice, whether by accident or through a flaky retry, must never count as two likes.

The one idea that resolves most of the hard parts of this design is splitting a single logical counter into many independent shards that can be incremented in parallel, and treating the displayed count as a fast, slightly approximate number that converges to the true total rather than something that has to be exact on every single read.

blocks.text: A user should be able to like a post, and doing so a second time should have no additional effect, the count only ever reflects one like per user per post. A user should be able to unlike a post they previously liked, removing their contribution to the count. Anyone viewing a post should see its current like count, and the requesting user's own client should know whether they personally have already liked it, so the UI can show the button in the right state.

blocks.alt: High write throughput on a single hot item, fast reads, strict idempotency, availability over exactness, and eventual exactness

blocks.text: Write throughput on one hot item is the defining constraint: an ordinary post might get a handful of likes an hour, a viral one can get tens of thousands a second, and the design has to handle both without treating the hot case as an outage. Reads need to stay fast regardless, nobody should wait on a database aggregation just to see a number on a screen. Idempotency is non-negotiable, since a double-counted like is a correctness bug a user could plausibly notice. And this system deliberately favors availability and a fast approximate answer over insisting on a perfectly exact count on every single read, as long as that approximate count keeps converging back to the truth.

blocks.text: The displayed like count is treated as approximate and eventually consistent, refreshed on the order of every one to two seconds, while whether a specific user has liked a specific post is treated as strongly consistent, since that is exactly what idempotency depends on. Every individual like and unlike is still recorded durably as an underlying fact, even though the fast aggregate count is optimized separately from that underlying record. Bot and spam filtering happens ahead of the counting pipeline entirely, this design assumes a request that reaches the Like API has already been judged legitimate.

blocks.text: Across the whole platform, total daily likes could easily run into the several billions. But the number that actually threatens this design is not that average, it is the single hottest post: a genuinely viral post can plausibly receive fifty thousand likes in a single second at its peak. No ordinary database row survives fifty thousand writes a second without serious contention. Split across a hundred shards, though, that becomes five hundred writes per second per shard, comfortably within what a single row can absorb, which is exactly the arithmetic that makes sharded counters the right answer here rather than an unnecessary complication.

blocks.text: A like request first passes through an idempotency check, confirming this specific user has not already liked this specific post, before touching the counter at all. Once past that check, the increment is routed to one shard of that post's counter, chosen so that load spreads evenly rather than concentrating. Each shard lives in a fast, in-memory store and is flushed to a durable counter store asynchronously, on a short interval rather than on every single write. Reads never sum shards live on every request, they hit a cached aggregate that is itself refreshed on that same short interval, and a background reconciliation job periodically checks that cached aggregate against the true underlying set of likes to correct any drift that crept in.

blocks.text: This is the load-bearing technique in the entire design. Instead of one row taking every single increment for a post, that post's count is represented as several independent shards, each of which can be incremented completely independently of the others, with no shared lock between them at all. Reading the true total just means summing every shard, which is cheap and can itself be cached rather than recomputed on every page view.

blocks.text: LikeRecord is the true, authoritative fact of who liked what, and it is what the reconciliation job ultimately checks against. CounterShard exists purely as a fast-path optimization on top of that fact, one row per shard per post, so a read never has to scan every LikeRecord for a popular post just to answer "how many."

blocks.text: This design deliberately keeps two representations of the same underlying fact: the individual LikeRecord rows, which are the source of truth and what idempotency and unlike both operate against, and the CounterShard aggregate, which is a derived, redundant value that exists purely because summing potentially millions of LikeRecord rows on every single read would be far too slow. Keeping these separate, rather than trying to make one representation serve both jobs well, is exactly what lets the read path stay fast and the write path stay correct at the same time.

A background job periodically compares the exact underlying like records against the currently stored aggregate and corrects it if the two have drifted apart

blocks.text: The happy path for an ordinary post is unremarkable: a like arrives, passes the idempotency check, increments a shard, done. The workflow worth walking through is what happens as a post crosses from ordinary into viral. Its write rate climbs past what its current small shard count can comfortably absorb, the scaling trigger in section 17 kicks in and grows its shard count, and new increments spread across the larger set of shards. Meanwhile the displayed count keeps refreshing on its normal interval throughout, briefly showing a number that is a few seconds behind reality during the busiest moments, then catching back up, which is precisely the trade-off this design accepts on purpose rather than trying to eliminate.

import threading
from typing import Dict, Set


# One post's counter, represented as several independent shards that
# can each be incremented without contending with each other.
class ShardedCounter:
    def __init__(self, shard_count: int):
        self._shards = [0] * shard_count           # independent counters
        self._locks = [threading.Lock() for _ in range(shard_count)]

    # Routes an increment to one shard, chosen by hashing the acting user's id
    # so load spreads evenly rather than concentrating on one shard.
    def increment(self, user_id: str) -> None:
        index = hash(user_id) % len(self._shards)      # which shard this user's action lands on
        with self._locks[index]:
            self._shards[index] += 1                       # bump that shard only

    def decrement(self, user_id: str) -> None:
        index = hash(user_id) % len(self._shards)      # same routing as increment
        with self._locks[index]:
            self._shards[index] -= 1                       # reduce that shard only

    # Sums every shard to produce the true current total. Cheap, but still
    # not free, which is exactly why callers cache this rather than call it
    # on every single read.
    def read_total(self) -> int:
        return sum(self._shards)                       # the true total right now


# Guarantees a like or unlike from the same user on the same post only
# ever takes effect once, regardless of retries or duplicate requests.
class LikeService:
    def __init__(self):
        self._liked_by_user_for_post: Dict[str, Set[str]] = {}   # postId -> set of userIds who have liked it
        self._counter_by_post: Dict[str, ShardedCounter] = {}       # postId -> its sharded counter
        self._lock = threading.Lock()

    def like(self, post_id: str, user_id: str) -> None:
        with self._lock:
            liked_users = self._liked_by_user_for_post.setdefault(post_id, set())   # this post's like set
            first_time = user_id not in liked_users   # false if userId was already present
            liked_users.add(user_id)
            if not first_time:
                return   # already liked, this call has no additional effect
            if post_id not in self._counter_by_post:
                self._counter_by_post[post_id] = ShardedCounter(self._default_shard_count_for(post_id))   # this post's counter
        self._counter_by_post[post_id].increment(user_id)   # count this genuinely new like

    def unlike(self, post_id: str, user_id: str) -> None:
        with self._lock:
            liked_users = self._liked_by_user_for_post.get(post_id)   # this post's like set, if it exists
            if liked_users is None or user_id not in liked_users:
                return   # was never liked, nothing to undo
            liked_users.discard(user_id)
            counter = self._counter_by_post.get(post_id)   # this post's counter
        if counter is not None:
            counter.decrement(user_id)   # reverse the earlier increment

    def approximate_count(self, post_id: str) -> int:
        with self._lock:
            counter = self._counter_by_post.get(post_id)   # this post's counter, if it exists
        return 0 if counter is None else counter.read_total()   # zero if nobody has liked it yet

    def _default_shard_count_for(self, post_id: str) -> int:
        return 8   # small default, grown dynamically as a post's write rate rises


if __name__ == "__main__":
    like_service = LikeService()   # the whole like counting system

    like_service.like("post-1", "alice")   # alice's first, genuine like
    print(f"After Alice likes: {like_service.approximate_count('post-1')}")

    like_service.like("post-1", "alice")   # alice retries or double taps
    print(f"After Alice likes again (duplicate): {like_service.approximate_count('post-1')}")

    like_service.like("post-1", "bob")   # bob's first, genuine like
    print(f"After Bob likes: {like_service.approximate_count('post-1')}")

    like_service.unlike("post-1", "bob")   # bob changes his mind
    print(f"After Bob unlikes: {like_service.approximate_count('post-1')}")

    like_service.unlike("post-1", "carol")   # carol never liked this post
    print(f"After Carol's no-op unlike: {like_service.approximate_count('post-1')}")

    is_one = like_service.approximate_count("post-1") == 1
    print(f"Final count is exactly one, from Alice's single genuine like: {str(is_one).lower()}")

items: Architecture: idempotency-checked likes routed to dynamically-sized sharded counters, flushed asynchronously to durable storage, read through a periodically refreshed cache.

Capacity: several billion daily likes platform-wide, a single viral post peaking at fifty thousand likes per second, spread across a hundred shards down to a manageable five hundred writes per second each.
The core technique: counter sharding, worked through with a concrete before-and-after write-throughput comparison.
Database: individual like records as the source of truth, a separate derived aggregate for fast reads, kept honest by a continuous reconciliation job.
Consistency: a deliberately split model, approximate for the displayed count, strongly consistent for per-user like state, since only the second one is what idempotency actually depends on.
Trade-offs: exact-but-slow versus approximate-but-fast counting, worked through with a direct three-way comparison table.
Production considerations: canarying scaling changes against a real trending post, and monitoring the reconciliation job's own load as a resource in its own right.
